title: The Karachi Hospital That Opened in 2007 Without a Cash Counter
dek: Twenty years after first imagining it, the surgeon Abdul Bari Khan and his friends opened a hospital in Korangi where no patient would be charged at all.

story.founder: Abdul Bari Khan (with friends from medical school)
story.company: Indus Hospital (later Indus Hospital & Health Network)
story.event: Opening a free, donation-funded hospital in Korangi with no cash counter
story.summary: In 2004 the cardiac surgeon Abdul Bari Khan and friends from medical school revived a long-held plan for a free hospital; with the Ruffaydah Foundation and the Islamic Mission Hospital Trust, which held a site in Korangi, Karachi, they began building in 2005. The Indus Hospital opened in 2007 with 150 beds and no cash counter, charging patients nothing and running on donations and zakat. By 2019 it had grown into a network of 12 hospitals.
paragraphs: In 2007 a 150-bed hospital opened in Korangi, a poor district of Karachi, without a cash counter. At the Indus Hospital no patient would be charged for anything, from primary care to the most expensive specialist treatment. "In 1987, I dreamed of a hospital that would provide the best care without any cash transactions," its co-founder, the cardiac surgeon Abdul Bari Khan, said in 2024.

He had seen what paying did to patients. He had watched families give up farm animals and homes to afford life-saving treatment, and, at Karachi's Civil Hospital, heart patients wait three years for surgery: "We knew many of these patients would never come back." A bomb blast in Karachi, which he dates to 1986, showed him a casualty department too small for the city, with victims treated on the floor; he and his colleagues raised the money, some of it from schoolchildren's collection boxes, for a 36-bed casualty ward. With fellow medical students he talked of one day building a free hospital of their own.

"In 2004 we regrouped and told one another that we had a dream and we had to realise it," Khan said. That year he set up the Ruffaydah Foundation and found a partner in the Islamic Mission Hospital Trust, which had a 20-acre site in Korangi and a hospital there that was not functioning. Building work began in May 2005. The rule was stark: no fees of any kind, with everything paid for by donations and zakat, the giving Islam requires of those who can afford it. Islamic scholars on the patient welfare team assess each patient's eligibility for zakat funds. Khan's view of the risk was simple: "If people have faith in you and you have established a credibility, the money will come."

The first patient came in 2007. Skilled staff were scarce at first, he later said, and the hospital ran without paper records, on software written by engineers Khan hired. By 2019, Anadolu Agency reported, the Korangi campus had 300 beds and saw more than 2,500 patients a day free of charge, donations met more than 90 per cent of a $130 million annual budget, and Indus ran a network of 12 hospitals. "We never turn people away," Khan said.

quote.text: Let us possess things in common; for birth is ours in common. Our relations with one another are like a stone arch, which would collapse if the stones did not mutually support each other, and which is upheld in this very way.
quote.work: Moral Letters to Lucilius (Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium)
quote.locator: Letter XCV, "On the Usefulness of Basic Principles", section 53
quote.source_title: Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 95, tr. Richard M. Gummere (Wikisource)
quote.connection: Seneca's arch stands only because each stone leans on the others. A hospital with no cash counter is that kind of structure: it holds while donors keep giving and patients keep trusting, which may be why Khan speaks of credibility before he speaks of money.

reflection: Twenty years passed between 1987, when Khan says he first imagined a hospital without cash transactions, and the day one opened. In between came other work, a casualty ward, a cardiac unit, and a year when old friends sat down and agreed to try. A long delay is not the same as giving up.

Seneca's arch is a fair picture of any work that depends on other people's trust: colleagues, supporters, the people you serve, the people at home. None of the stones holds itself up. If something you carry feels heavy this morning, it may be that you are trying to be the whole arch.
invitation: Think of one person whose work quietly holds up yours, a colleague or someone at home. Tell them today, in a sentence, what their part makes possible.

cross_checks.claim: The Indus Hospital opened in Korangi, Karachi, in 2007 with 150 beds
The hospital had no cash counter and charged patients nothing
It was set up with the Ruffaydah Foundation and the Islamic Mission Hospital Trust
It runs on donations and zakat
A 1986 Karachi bomb blast was a turning point that led Khan to work on emergency care
By 2019 Indus ran a network of about a dozen hospitals

research_notes: The blast: Khan himself (Pakistan & Gulf Economist 2021) and Eastern Eye date it to 1986 in Saddar, and Nukta calls it the 1986 Bohri Bazaar bombing; Anadolu Agency gives 1987 and 200 dead, while Eastern Eye gives more than 70 dead and about 250 injured. The story says 'which he dates to 1986' and gives no death toll. The site: the Pakistan & Gulf Economist (2018, 2021) says the Islamic Mission Hospital Trust held a 20-acre site in Korangi with a non-functional hospital that became The Indus Hospital; Anadolu Agency says an expatriate Pakistani donated the land. The story follows the Trust account, which two Gulf Economist pieces and Khan's own interview support. Beds at opening: 150 in Nukta, the Gulf Economist (2017, 2021) and Anadolu Agency; the Gulf Economist's 2018 profile says 350, apparently planned capacity; 150 is used. Founders: Anadolu Agency says Khan and three college friends; the story says 'friends' and 'fellow medical students' without a number. The Foundation is spelled Ruffaydah (Eastern Eye, Gulf Economist 2017) and Rufaydah (Gulf Economist 2018); the first is used. Patient volumes disagree (Anadolu Agency 2019: about 350,000 a month across the network; Eastern Eye 2019: about 200,000 a month) and are left out; the 2019 figures used (300 beds, 2,500 patients a day at the main campus, $130 million budget, over 90 per cent from donations) are attributed to Anadolu Agency. Profiles in Dawn (2012, 2019) and The Express Tribune were read where possible but block the verifier, so they are not cited; Dawn's 2012 profile also says construction began in May 2005, consistent with the Gulf Economist. 'Twenty years' in the reflection runs from Khan's stated 1987 to the 2007 opening. The Seneca passage concerns human fellowship in general and is applied here by analogy.
